bill.title: SAFE Drugs Act of 2026
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 524.
subjects: Department of Health and Human Services
Drug safety, medical device, and laboratory regulation
bill.officialSummary: Safeguarding Americans from Fraudulent and Experimental Drugs Act of 2026 or the SAFE Drugs Act of 2026 This bill provides for increased oversight of drug compounding and imposes statutory limits on compounded drugs that are essentially copies of commercially available drugs. Currently, subject to certain requirements, compounded drugs (i.e., drugs that are mixed or altered to meet patient needs) do not require Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval. Additional limits apply to the compounding of drugs that are essentially copies of commercially available drug products. Under the bill, a compounded drug is essentially a copy of a commercially available drug product if (1) the compounded drug contains any active ingredient found in a commercially available drug product, and (2) there is no change made for an individual patient that results in a significant difference between the compounded drug and the commercially available drug. (The FDA’s current definition of the term also addresses dosage strength and route of administration.) The bill increases the frequency at which a licensed pharmacist or physician may compound a drug that is essentially a copy of a commercially available drug to 20 times per month. Current FDA policy allows four such prescriptions per month. The bill also imposes annual reporting requirements on physicians, facilities, and pharmacies (except hospital-based pharmacies) that compound certain drug products for out-of-state patients more than 20 times per month. Further, the bill subjects certain large-scale outsourcing facilities (i.e., FDA-registered facilities that compound in bulk) to regular inspection and reporting requirements.

classification.plainSummary: This bill tightens federal oversight of drug compounding—the practice of mixing or altering medications to meet individual patient needs. It redefines when a compounded drug is considered an "essentially a copy" of an FDA-approved commercial product, raises the monthly limit on such compounding from 4 to 20 prescriptions, and requires annual reporting by physicians and facilities that compound drugs for out-of-state patients more than 20 times per month. Large-scale compounding facilities would face regular inspections and new reporting obligations.

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates compounding pharmacies and outsourcing facilities, imposing new definitions, frequency limits, reporting requirements, and inspection obligations on drug compounding operations.
Physicians who compound drugs or prescribe compounded medications face new reporting requirements if they exceed the monthly threshold for out-of-state patients.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill would provide for increased oversight of drug compounding and place statutory limits on compounded drugs that are essentially copies of commercially available drugs.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who takes a medicine. People who work in health care, and their patients.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in which medicines you can be given. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
